title.text: Conditional probability and Bayes: updating beliefs with evidence

objects.text: A test finds 90% of sick people and wrongly flags 10% of healthy people. You test positive. How likely are you sick?

Mathematics for AI and Machine Learning  |  Session 15 of 18  |  Probability and statistics
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome to Session 15, the last session on probability itself. Today is about updating a belief when evidence arrives. We start with a famous surprise: a test that finds 90 percent of sick people, and wrongly flags 10 percent of healthy people, says positive, and the chance you are sick is under 10 percent.

Then we turn the same rule into a small spam filter. We close with how to read a probability that an AI model gives you.

title.text: Today in one view: what you will leave with

objects.text: By the end of today you can
Read joint, marginal and conditional probabilities from a table of counts, and test for independence
Apply Bayes theorem with natural frequencies, naming the prior, likelihood and posterior
Build a small Naive Bayes spam classifier by hand and in code, and read a model probability with care

slides.notes:
By the end of today you can do three things. Read joint, marginal and conditional probabilities from a table of counts, and test whether two events are independent. Apply Bayes theorem using natural frequencies, and name the prior, the likelihood and the posterior. And build a small Naive Bayes spam filter by hand and in code, and then read a probability from a model with care.

That includes the caution that a fluent answer from a language model is not a probability that it is true.

title.text:
Your two hours: counts,
Bayes, a spam filter, then AI

objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: Tables of counts first, then Bayes with natural frequencies, then the spam filter by hand and in the lab.

slides.notes:
We start with ten minutes of recall from Session 14 and the question about a positive medical test. Then thirty-five minutes of concepts, a picture first and a hand example after it. After the break you spend forty-five minutes in the lab, in Python or in a spreadsheet, on the same numbers.

We finish with where this appears in AI, an exit check, and saving your work.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  What does lowering the temperature do to the next-word probabilities?
2.  What does a standard error measure?
3.  An A/B test gives p = 0.039. What does that mean?

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 14. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. What does lowering the temperature do to the next-word probabilities? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. It sharpens them: the top word gets more probability, and answers repeat more.

Question two. What does a standard error measure? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. How much a sample mean wanders from sample to sample: sigma divided by the square root of n.

Question three. An A/B test gives p = 0.039. What does that mean? Think about your own task as you answer.

A good answer is this. A gap this large would be rare if there were truly no difference. It is not a 3.9% chance that the feature does nothing.

If an answer was missing, do not worry. Your notes from last class have it. Now to today.

title.text: Answers to the three questions from Session 14

rows.text: What does lowering the temperature do to the next-word probabilities?
It sharpens them: the top word gets more probability, and answers repeat more.
What does a standard error measure?
How much a sample mean wanders from sample to sample: sigma divided by the square root of n.
An A/B test gives p = 0.039. What does that mean?
A gap this large would be rare if there were truly no difference. It is not a 3.9% chance that the feature does nothing.

objects.text: If an answer surprised you, look back at Session 14 before the lab.

slides.notes:
Here are the short answers. Lowering the temperature sharpens the next-word probabilities, so the top word gets more and answers repeat. The standard error measures how much a sample mean wanders from sample to sample, and it is sigma over the square root of n. And a p-value of 0.039 says that a gap this large would be rare if there were truly no difference.

It does not say there is a 3.9 percent chance that the feature does nothing. Check your own answers against these.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: P(A | B): the probability of A once we know B happened.
Two events are independent when knowing one does not change the probability of the other.
The belief before evidence, the chance of the evidence if the hypothesis is true (for a test: its sensitivity), and the updated belief.
The rule P(H | E) = P(E | H) P(H) / P(E): the posterior from the likelihood, the prior and the evidence.
A classifier that multiplies per-word likelihoods, naively treating the words as independent.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Conditional probability. P(A | B): the probability of A once we know B happened.

Independence. Two events are independent when knowing one does not change the probability of the other.

Prior, likelihood and posterior. The belief before evidence, the chance of the evidence if the hypothesis is true (for a test: its sensitivity), and the updated belief.

Bayes' theorem. The rule P(H | E) = P(E | H) P(H) / P(E): the posterior from the likelihood, the prior and the evidence.

Naive Bayes classifier. A classifier that multiplies per-word likelihoods, naively treating the words as independent.

title.text:
A table of counts shows joint
and marginal probabilities

objects.alt: A table of counts shows joint and marginal probabilities

objects.text: Illustrative: 100 emails, 40 spam and 60 ham, sorted by whether they contain the word "free".

runs.text: Joint probability: P(spam and free) = 28 / 100 = 0.28 (gold).
Marginal probability: one event on its own, from a row or column total. P(free) = 34 / 100 = 0.34.

slides.notes:
Here is a small table of counts. It is illustrative, made up to show the arithmetic. One hundred emails, forty of them spam and sixty ham, and in each row we count how many contain the word free. The gold cell is a joint probability: twenty-eight emails are both spam and contain free, so the probability of both is 0.28.

A marginal probability comes from a total in the margin of the table. Thirty-four emails contain free, so the marginal probability of free is 0.34. Forty are spam, so the marginal probability of spam is 0.40. What is the marginal probability of ham?

title.text:
A conditional probability looks only at
the emails where the condition holds

objects.alt: A conditional probability looks only at the emails where the condition holds

objects.text: Given that an email contains "free", only the 34 emails in the first column matter.

runs.text: The two are different questions with different answers.

slides.notes:
Now a conditional probability. We write P of A given B, with a vertical bar. It means: restrict attention to the cases where B is true, and ask how often A is true among them. Suppose an email contains the word free. Only the 34 emails in the first column remain, and 28 of them are spam, so P of spam given free is 28 over 34, 0.8235.

Turn it around. Among the 40 spam emails, 28 contain free, so P of free given spam is 0.70. The two numbers differ, and mixing them up is the commonest mistake in this topic.

title.text: Joint, marginal and conditional probability

rows.text: The joint probability: both events happen.
The marginal probability of the condition.
The conditional probability: A given B.

objects.text: The product rule is the same formula rearranged: 0.34 × 0.8235 = 0.28.

slides.notes:
Here are the formulas. The conditional probability of A given B is the joint probability of A and B, divided by the marginal probability of B. That is the same as our counting argument, with the counts divided by 100. For our emails, 0.28 divided by 0.34 gives 0.8235.

Rearrange it and you get the product rule: the joint probability is P of B times P of A given B. Check it: 0.34 times 0.8235 is 0.28. This rule is the engine behind Bayes theorem.

title.text:
Independent events do not change each other's
probability: "free" and spam are not independent

objects.alt: Independent events do not change each other's probability: "free" and spam are not independent

objects.text: Independent means P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).

runs.text: If independent: P(spam) × P(free) = 0.40 × 0.34 = 0.136, so 13.6 emails.
Observed: 28 emails. Far more than 13.6.
So the word carries information about spam. A filter can use it.

slides.notes:
Two events are independent when knowing one tells you nothing about the other. Two dice are independent: the first die does not change the second. Then the probability of both is the product of the two probabilities. Test it on our emails. If free and spam were independent, we would expect 0.4 times 0.34 of the 100 emails to be spam containing free, which is 13.6.

We actually observe 28. The gap tells us the word is informative, which is exactly why a spam filter can use it.

title.text:
Natural frequencies: of 1,000 people, 9 sick people
test positive and 99 healthy people test positive

objects.alt: Natural frequencies: of 1,000 people, 9 sick people test positive and 99 healthy people test positive

objects.text: Illustrative: 1% sick. Sensitivity 90% (sick found). False positive rate 10% (healthy flagged).

slides.notes:
Now the famous surprise, with natural frequencies. Natural frequencies means we count people instead of juggling percentages. All numbers are illustrative. Take a thousand people. One percent are sick, that is ten. The test catches ninety percent of them, a rate called the sensitivity, so nine test positive.

Of the 990 healthy people, ten percent are wrongly flagged, which is 99 people. That ten percent is the false positive rate. Now you test positive. You are one of the gold boxes: 9 plus 99, 108 people. Only 9 of them are sick. What fraction is that?

title.text:
A positive test moves the belief from 1%
to 8.3%, and a second positive test to 45%

objects.alt: A positive test moves the belief from 1% to 8.3%, and a second positive test to 45%

objects.text: Chance of being sick: 9 / (9 + 99) = 0.0833 after one positive test.

runs.text: Most positives come from the many healthy people.
A second positive test lifts it to 45%, if its error is independent of the first.
Evidence updates a belief. It does not replace it.

slides.notes:
Here is the answer as a picture. Before the test, your chance of being sick is the prevalence, 1 percent. After one positive test it is 9 out of 108, which is 8.3 percent. Most positive results come from the huge group of healthy people, even though each has only a ten percent chance of a false alarm.

If you take a second, independent test and it is positive too, the belief rises to 45 percent. This assumes the second test makes errors independent of the first. Repeat tests on the same person often do not. Evidence updates a belief. It does not replace the prior. That is Bayes theorem in action.

title.text:
Bayes' theorem: prior, likelihood,
evidence and posterior

objects.alt: Bayes' theorem: prior, likelihood, evidence and posterior

rows.text: Prior: belief in the hypothesis H (sick) before the evidence E (a positive test).
Likelihood (here the sensitivity): how likely the evidence is if H is true.
Marginal likelihood of the evidence, also just called the evidence: 0.9 × 0.01 + 0.1 × 0.99.
Posterior: the updated belief after the evidence.

objects.text: The same 9 / 108 as the natural frequencies, with probabilities instead of counts.

slides.notes:
Here is the rule with proper names. We want the posterior, P of H given E, the belief after the evidence. It equals the likelihood, P of E given H, times the prior, P of H, divided by the evidence, P of E. The evidence is the overall chance of a positive test: ninety percent of one percent, plus ten percent of ninety-nine percent, which is 0.108.

The top is 0.9 times 0.01, which is 0.009. Divide, and you get 0.0833. It is the same 9 out of 108 you got by counting people.

title.text:
The most common mistake is
to swap P(E | H) and P(H | E)

objects.text: P(positive | sick) = 0.90

runs.text: How well the test finds sick people
The likelihood, set by the test maker

objects.text: P(sick | positive) = 0.083

runs.text: What you want to know after a positive result
The posterior, which also needs the prior

objects.text: Ignoring the prior (the base rate) is called base rate neglect.

slides.notes:
Here is the mistake in one slide. On the left, ninety percent is the probability of a positive test given that you are sick. That is the likelihood, and it describes the test. On the right, 8.3 percent is the probability that you are sick given a positive test.

That is the posterior, and it also depends on how rare the disease is. People often read the first number as if it were the second. Forgetting the base rate in this way is called base rate neglect. Which one does a patient actually care about?

title.text:
A tiny table of word counts is all
a Naive Bayes spam filter needs

objects.alt: A tiny table of word counts is all a Naive Bayes spam filter needs

objects.text: Illustrative training counts: how many emails of each class contain each word.

runs.text: Prior: P(spam) = 40 / 100 = 0.4 and P(ham) = 0.6.
"free" and "prize" point to spam. "meeting" points to ham.
The gold zero is a problem: no ham email contained "prize".

slides.notes:
Here is the training data for a tiny spam filter. It is illustrative. Out of 100 training emails, 40 are spam and 60 are ham. For three words we count how many emails of each class contain the word. The priors come straight from the class sizes: 0.4 for spam and 0.6 for ham.

Free and prize lean to spam, and meeting leans to ham. Now look at the gold zero. No ham email contained prize. That sounds harmless, but a zero will wreck a multiplication, as we are about to see.

title.text:
Add-one smoothing turns each count
into a likelihood and removes the zero

objects.alt: Add-one smoothing turns each count into a likelihood and removes the zero

objects.text: Likelihood = (count + 1) / (emails in the class + 2). This is add-one (Laplace) smoothing.

runs.text: A zero would make it impossible for any email with "prize" to be ham.

slides.notes:
To turn counts into likelihoods we use a small trick called add-one smoothing, also known as Laplace smoothing. Add one to the count, and add two to the class size. For free in spam that gives 29 over 42, which is 0.690. For prize in ham, instead of zero we get 1 over 62, which is 0.016: small but not zero.

Without smoothing, one unseen word would force the ham probability to exactly zero, and no other evidence could ever win it back. A filter should never be that certain from a few emails.

title.text:
Naive Bayes: multiply the prior
by one likelihood per word

objects.alt: Naive Bayes: multiply the prior by one likelihood per word

rows.text: The prior of the class c (spam or ham).
The smoothed likelihood of word w present. For an absent word use 1 - P(w | c).
The factor for word w: P(w | c) if w is in the email, 1 - P(w | c) if not.
Multiply over all the words. "Naive": treat the words as independent.

objects.text: The words are not truly independent, so the method is naive, yet it works well for spam.

slides.notes:
Here is Naive Bayes. For each class, multiply the prior by one likelihood for each word. A word that is present contributes its likelihood. A word that is absent contributes one minus its likelihood. The word naive refers to the big simplifying assumption: given the class, the words are treated as independent of each other.

That is not true, free and prize often come together, but it makes the arithmetic tiny. Then the posterior is the spam score divided by the sum of both scores. The next two slides do it by hand.

title.text:
By hand, email 1 has "free" and "prize" but
no "meeting": spam with probability 0.9955

objects.alt: By hand, email 1 has "free" and "prize" but no "meeting": spam with probability 0.9955

objects.text: Multiply down each column, then divide the spam score by the total.

runs.text: Spam score 0.12166. Ham score 0.00055.
Strong evidence: spam by a wide margin.

slides.notes:
Email one contains free and prize, but not meeting. Start each column with the prior. Multiply by the likelihood of free, then of prize, then by one minus the likelihood of meeting, because meeting is absent. Spam comes to 0.12166. Ham comes to a tiny 0.00055, dragged down by prize, which almost never appears in ham.

Divide the spam score by the total and the posterior is 0.9955. The filter is very sure this one is spam.

title.text:
Email 2 has "free" and "meeting" but no
"prize": the filter leans to ham (33% spam)

objects.alt: Email 2 has "free" and "meeting" but no "prize": the filter leans to ham (33% spam)

objects.text: Same method. The word "meeting" and the missing "prize" now point to ham.

runs.text: Spam score 0.01644. Ham score 0.03332.
Not sure: about one chance in three of spam.

slides.notes:
Email two says free lunch at the meeting. It contains free and meeting, but not prize. The same method. Multiply the prior by 0.690 for free, 0.119 for meeting, and one minus 0.5 for the missing prize. Spam scores 0.01644. For ham we have 0.113 for free, 0.5 for meeting and 0.984 for the missing prize, and the score is 0.03332.

The posterior for spam is 0.3304. A real filter would use a threshold, say flag above 0.9, so this email goes to the inbox. Which words pushed it towards ham?

title.text:
Many words multiply many small
numbers, so we add logarithms instead

objects.alt: Many words multiply many small numbers, so we add logarithms instead

objects.text: Session 1 gave us logarithms, and Session 12 gave us the stable softmax. Both are used here.

runs.text: ln(score(spam)) = -2.107. ln(score(ham)) = -7.512.
Softmax of these two numbers gives 0.9955, the same posterior.

slides.notes:
A real spam filter uses thousands of words, so it multiplies thousands of numbers below one, and the product underflows to zero. The fix uses two tools from earlier sessions. The logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms, so we add instead of multiplying. Then softmax, in its stable form, turns the log scores back into probabilities.

For email one the log scores are -2.107 and -7.512, and softmax gives 0.9955. It is the same posterior, now safe for long emails.

title.text: Bridge: Naive Bayes from counts in NumPy

runs.text: spam = np.array([28, 20, 4])
ham = np.array([6, 0, 30])
ls = (spam + 1) / 42
has = np.array([1, 1, 0])
ps = 0.4 * np.prod(np.where(has == 1, ls, 1 - ls))
ph = 0.6 * np.prod(np.where(has == 1, lh, 1 - lh))
ps / (ps + ph)

objects.text: In plain words

runs.text: Lines 1 and 2: the word counts for free, prize and meeting.
Lines 3 and 4: smoothed likelihoods.
Line 5: 1 if the word is in the email, 0 if not.
Lines 6 and 7: where picks the likelihood if present, one minus it if absent. prod multiplies.
Line 8: the posterior of spam.

slides.notes:
Here is the same filter in code. The counts go into two arrays, and the smoothed likelihoods are one line each. A vector called present records which words are in the email. The where function picks the likelihood for a present word and one minus the likelihood for an absent word, and prod multiplies them.

Then we multiply by the prior. The last line divides the spam score by the total, and for present equal to 1, 1, 0 it gives 0.9955. In the spreadsheet you build the same steps in a table.

slides.notes:
Use this table as your checkpoint. Each row names what you compute and the number you should see. The conditional probabilities come from the table of counts. The medical posterior is 0.0833 after one positive test and 0.45 after two. The two spam posteriors are 0.9955 and 0.3304.

title.text:
Errors you will meet, what
they mean and what to do

rows.text: You divided by 40 instead of 34. Divide by the emails with the condition.
You used 0.1 as P(E). Add both routes: 0.9 × 0.01 + 0.1 × 0.99 = 0.108. (Forgetting the false positives gives 1.0.)
RuntimeWarning: divide by zero in log
A likelihood is 0. Use the smoothed likelihood (count + 1) / (n + 2).
The ham score was not added to the denominator.
Likelihood of an absent word is wrong
Use 1 - P(word | class) for a word that is not in the email.

slides.notes:
Here are the errors you will probably meet. If P of spam given free comes out as 0.7, you divided by the number of spam emails instead of the number of emails with the word. If the posterior is 0.09 instead of 0.0833, you used 0.1 as the evidence, so add both routes to a positive test.

Forgetting the false positives altogether would give 1.0. A divide by zero warning means an unsmoothed likelihood of zero. A posterior above one means the denominator is missing the ham score. And for an absent word, use one minus the likelihood. Read the message first.

title.text:
Where this appears in AI: spam
filters and medical-risk classifiers

objects.alt: Where this appears in AI: spam filters and medical-risk classifiers

objects.text: A prior, likelihoods and a posterior run in many classifiers.

runs.text: Sahami and colleagues published Bayesian junk email filtering in 1998.
A medical-risk classifier needs the base rate too.
Chat assistants are language models, not Naive Bayes.

slides.notes:
Here is where today appears. Spam filtering with Bayes rule was published by Sahami and colleagues in 1998, and the pattern of a prior, likelihoods and a posterior sits in many classifiers since. A medical-risk classifier works the same way: its probability needs the base rate to mean anything.

Chat assistants such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude are not Naive Bayes classifiers. They are language models, but they still output probabilities, and the next two slides show how to read those.

title.text:
Where this appears in AI: a stated probability
should be checked against how often it is right

objects.alt: Where this appears in AI: a stated probability should be checked against how often it is right

objects.text: Illustrative (made-up) check: the model says 90% but is right 75% of the time.

runs.text: Calibrated: stated probability equals the hit rate.
Guo and colleagues, 2017: many neural networks are over-confident.

slides.notes:
How should you read a probability from a model?

Compare it with how often the model is right. This table is illustrative. Among 200 cases where the model said ninety percent, it was right 150 times, which is 75 percent. That model is over-confident. When stated probability matches the observed rate, we say the model is calibrated.

Guo and colleagues reported in 2017 that many modern neural networks are over-confident. So a ninety percent from a model is not a guarantee. It is a claim to be tested against a record of outcomes.

title.text:
Where this appears in AI: a fluent
answer is not a probability that it is true

objects.text: What the model computes

runs.text: The probability of the next token given the text
High for a likely wording

objects.text: What it does not give you

runs.text: The probability that the statement is true
A warning that a fluent sentence is false

objects.text: Check important claims against a source or your own calculation.

slides.notes:
A caution that matters for everything you do with language models. A model computes the probability of the next token given the text so far. A high probability means the wording is a likely continuation. It does not mean the statement is true. Researchers have documented fluent but false answers, often called hallucinations.

So the fluency of an answer is not evidence. For important claims, check a source or redo the calculation, just as you did with the medical test. Which of your own uses of an assistant needs this check?

title.text:
Where this appears in AI: check
an assistant on the medical test

objects.text: 8 minutes
Check an AI assistant
Ask an AI assistant the medical test question with our made-up numbers.

runs.text: Say: 1% are sick, 90% of sick people test positive, and 10% of healthy people do too.
Ask: I tested positive. How likely am I sick?
Compare with 9 / 108 = 0.0833.
Ask how sure it is.

objects.text: You keep
A note: its answer, the correct 8.3%, and what its confidence meant.

slides.notes:
A short activity. Give any AI assistant the medical test numbers, one percent prevalence, ninety percent of sick people found, ten percent of healthy people flagged, and ask how likely you are to be sick after a positive test. The right answer is 9 out of 108, 0.0833.

See whether the assistant gets it, and whether it shows its steps. Then ask how sure it is, and think about what that statement means. Use only made-up numbers like these, and never paste confidential data.

title.text: Exit check: three questions

rows.text: In the 100 emails, P(free | spam) = 0.70 and P(spam | free) = 0.82. Why do they differ?
They condition on different groups: 40 spam emails against 34 emails with the word.
A disease affects 1 in 1,000. A test finds 99% of sick people and wrongly flags 1% of healthy people. Roughly how likely is a positive person to be sick?
About 9%. Of 1,000 people, about 1 sick positive and about 10 healthy positives: 1 / 11.
A language model gives a fluent answer. Is that the probability that it is true?
No. It reflects how likely the wording is. Check the claim.

slides.notes:
Three questions to finish. First, the two conditional probabilities differ because they restrict to different groups: forty spam emails against 34 emails with the word. Second, a disease in one in a thousand, with a test that finds 99 percent and flags one percent of healthy people. Of a thousand people about one sick person tests positive and about ten healthy people do, so roughly one in eleven, about nine percent.

Third, a fluent answer is not the probability that it is true. Write your answers in your lab file.
